title: Testing Coroutines & Flows
scopeHtml: Scope: runTest and virtual time, test dispatchers, scheduler sharing, setMain, dispatcher injection, StateFlow/Turbine testing, debounce/cancellation/exception tests, flakiness, and MockK vs fakes. Versions referenced: kotlinx-coroutines-test 1.7 to 1.10, Turbine 1.2.x.

notes.title: runTest and virtual time
notes.html:
The idea. A normal test with delay(10_000) would sit and wait ten real seconds. runTest swaps the clock for a fake one. Delays do not wait; the fake clock just JUMPS ahead to the next scheduled task. Ten "seconds" pass in milliseconds.

Mechanism. runTest { } creates a TestScope with a TestCoroutineScheduler and a StandardTestDispatcher. The scheduler holds a priority queue of tasks keyed by virtual time. When the test body suspends (on delay, join, await), the scheduler runs queued tasks; when nothing is runnable it advances virtual time to the earliest delayed task. delay(10_000) just enqueues "resume at t+10_000", so the scheduler jumps there immediately.

What runTest does (Q652), start to finish.

  1. Creates the TestScope (or uses the receiver) and runs the body as a coroutine on the test dispatcher.
  2. Drives the scheduler: runs tasks, skips virtual time, until the body completes.
  3. After the body finishes, runs remaining tasks scheduled for the current time and children launched with launch, waits for children to complete (the test is done when ALL children are done).
  4. Cancels backgroundScope coroutines.
  5. Reports uncaught exceptions from children; throws UncompletedCoroutinesError if work remains that cannot complete (a never-ending child).
  6. Real async work (a real thread, Dispatchers.IO, a Room callback) is NOT controlled by virtual time: runTest waits for it in real time up to the timeout. Mixing real threads with virtual delays gives races.

Timeout (Q634). The default is 10 seconds of REAL time (Kotlin coroutines 1.7+; earlier versions used 60 s and dispatchTimeoutMs). It is not virtual time, because virtual time is skipped. Change: runTest(timeout = 30.seconds) { }. (Confirm in your version's docs.)

Hanging tests (Q653). Symptom: CI job stuck, After waiting for 10s, the test coroutine is not completing, there were active child jobs. Common causes: a child with an infinite loop (while(true) { delay }) launched in the test scope rather than backgroundScope; a collect on a never-completing StateFlow; waiting on a channel nobody sends to; real Dispatchers.IO work never done. Fix: use backgroundScope for collectors and infinite jobs; inject test dispatchers; print coroutineContext.job.children.

Real examples. Google's Architecture Samples and NowInAndroid tests use runTest for every ViewModel test. A 20-minute CI test suite shrank to seconds after removing Thread.sleep for runTest.

Analogy. Watching a film on fast-forward: the story is the same, you just skip the empty waiting scenes.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing the timeout is virtual.
  • Launching infinite collectors in this instead of backgroundScope.
  • Expecting runTest to control Dispatchers.IO work.

notes.title: Test dispatchers and the scheduler
notes.html:
StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher (Q635).

  • StandardTestDispatcher: queues coroutines; nothing runs until the test yields (advanceUntilIdle, runCurrent, delay, join). Deterministic, mimics real dispatchers where launch returns before the child runs. DEFAULT choice.
  • UnconfinedTestDispatcher: starts coroutines eagerly (like Dispatchers.Unconfined) up to the first suspension. Convenient for "just collect values" but changes ordering and can hide races (see below).

Scheduler sharing (Q636). TestScope owns a TestCoroutineScheduler. A dispatcher has a scheduler. If two dispatchers (the one in runTest and the one given to setMain or injected into a repository) have DIFFERENT schedulers, each has its own virtual clock; advanceUntilIdle() on one does not drive the other and delays never meet. Fix: create dispatchers from the SAME scheduler: StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler), or let Dispatchers.setMain(...) before runTest (runTest picks up the Main test dispatcher's scheduler automatically).

Controlling time (Q637).

  • advanceUntilIdle(): run everything that is runnable or scheduled, advancing time as needed, until no tasks remain. (Never ends with infinite periodic work.)
  • advanceTimeBy(1000): run tasks scheduled strictly BEFORE currentTime + 1000; tasks at exactly +1000 are NOT run. Follow with runCurrent() to run tasks at the new current time.
  • runCurrent(): run tasks scheduled for the current virtual time, without moving time.
  • currentTime reads the clock.
launch { delay(1000); println("A") }
advanceTimeBy(1000)  // A not printed (task is at exactly 1000)
runCurrent()         // now A prints

Virtual time boundary (Q650). withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { delay(1000) } in production code uses REAL IO dispatcher and real time: the test cannot skip it. Bug pattern: hard-coded dispatcher. The fix is to inject (below) so the test supplies the test dispatcher.

Dispatcher choice hides state (Q655). With Unconfined, a stateIn/StateFlow collector sees every intermediate state because everything runs eagerly; with Standard, conflation may skip states. Tests green on Unconfined may hide bugs that real dispatchers expose. Trade-off: use Standard by default (production-like), Unconfined only where eager start is needed (collect-into-list before triggering).

Analogy. A conductor (scheduler) with a baton: all musicians (dispatchers) must follow the same conductor, otherwise each plays to their own tempo.

Common interview traps.

  • Two schedulers in one test.
  • Thinking advanceTimeBy(1000) runs tasks at exactly 1000.
  • Using Unconfined everywhere and missing ordering bugs.
  • Production code hard-coding Dispatchers.IO / Default.

notes.title: Main dispatcher rule and injecting dispatchers
notes.html:
The crash (Q638). Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize. For tests Dispatchers.setMain from kotlinx-coroutines-test module can be used. On the JVM unit test there's no Android Looper, so Dispatchers.Main has no implementation; viewModelScope uses Dispatchers.Main.immediate.

Proper fix: a JUnit rule.

class MainDispatcherRule(
    val dispatcher: TestDispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher()
) : TestWatcher() {
    override fun starting(d: Description) = Dispatchers.setMain(dispatcher)
    override fun finished(d: Description) = Dispatchers.resetMain()
}

Always resetMain() in cleanup; otherwise one test's dispatcher leaks into the next and causes flaky failures. Dependency: kotlinx-coroutines-test.

Injecting dispatchers (Q639). Production code that writes withContext(Dispatchers.IO) cannot be tested virtually. Inject:

class Repo(private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) {
    suspend fun load() = withContext(io) { ... }
}
// Hilt: @Qualifier annotation class IoDispatcher; @Provides @IoDispatcher fun io() = Dispatchers.IO

In tests pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler). Benefits: determinism, virtual time, and a single place to change threading policy.

Spot-the-bug (Q640). ViewModel test fails because: no setMain; viewModel.state.value read before advanceUntilIdle(); runTest and MainDispatcherRule have separate schedulers; or an Unconfined dispatcher used in the rule but Standard in the repository.

Real examples. Google's Android Architecture docs recommend injecting dispatchers and using MainDispatcherRule; Hilt @IoDispatcher qualifiers are a standard pattern in NowInAndroid.

Analogy. A kitchen where the stove is plugged in through an adapter: tests swap the adapter for a safe fake stove without rewiring the kitchen.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting resetMain().
  • Injecting a dispatcher but also hard-coding Dispatchers.Default elsewhere.
  • Using Dispatchers.setMain AFTER creating the ViewModel.

notes.title: Testing StateFlow and Turbine
notes.html:
ViewModel with stateIn (Q641). uiState built with WhileSubscribed(5_000) only starts when someone collects. A test that reads .value without a collector sees Loading (the initial value) forever. Fix: subscribe in backgroundScope:

@Test fun loads() = runTest {
    val vm = MyVm(FakeRepo())
    backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.uiState.collect {} }
    advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals(Content(items), vm.uiState.value)
}

backgroundScope is cancelled automatically at the end, so the infinite collector does not hang the test.

Turbine (Q642). Cash App's library: flow.test { awaitItem(); awaitComplete(); cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents() }. It collects into an unlimited Channel in the background and lets you assert events one at a time with timeouts (timeouts are wall-clock, 3 s by default; newer versions use the scheduler). APIs: awaitItem(), awaitError(), awaitComplete(), expectNoEvents(), skipItems(n), cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents(), expectMostRecentItem(). It FAILS at the end of test if there are unconsumed events: that catches stray emissions that toList() hides. Prefer it over toList() in a background coroutine because it gives ordering assertions and explicit failure instead of a race.

Pitfalls (Q643). A StateFlow conflates: if two states are set quickly (A then B before the collector runs), the collector sees only B, so awaitItem() for A times out. Also the initial value is always the first item. "Unconsumed events" error arises when more items arrive than you awaited. Robust assertions: use expectMostRecentItem(), or awaitItem() in a loop until a predicate; or run with Unconfined so every state is observed; or assert on the final state instead of the intermediate states.

SharedFlow events (Q654). A replay-0 SharedFlow drops events emitted before a collector subscribes. Test bug: calling vm.onClick() THEN vm.events.test { awaitItem() } times out. Subscribe first (test { block or backgroundScope collector), then trigger, then await.

Real examples. NowInAndroid, Cash App, and Square test ViewModels with Turbine. Flaky "Unconsumed events" failures appear when ViewModel emits an extra Loading state.

Analogy. Turbine is a tape recorder next to a talk show: it records every sentence in order so you can check the sequence afterwards, and flags it if there is audio you never listened to.

Common interview traps.

  • Reading .value with WhileSubscribed and no collector.
  • Asserting every intermediate StateFlow state.
  • Triggering an event before subscribing to a replay-0 SharedFlow.
  • Launching the collector in this rather than backgroundScope so the test hangs.

notes.title: Time-dependent logic
notes.html:
Debounce and delays (Q644). Ambiguous requirement: "debounce search 300 ms". Clarify: does a new key reset the timer, does the first key fire immediately, what happens at exactly 300? Test with virtual time:

vm.onQuery("a"); advanceTimeBy(299); vm.onQuery("ab")
advanceTimeBy(300)        // runs tasks before +300
runCurrent()              // include the boundary task
assertEquals(listOf("ab"), repo.queries)

Time sources (Q656). Inject whatever reads time:

  • withTimeout: just use delay in the fake to exceed the limit; assert TimeoutCancellationException.
  • Backoff retries: fake fails N times; use advanceTimeBy to check delay at each attempt (500, 1000, 2000) and currentTime.
  • Polling: advanceTimeBy(interval * 3 + 1) and assert call count; cancel the poller.
  • Cache TTL: inject a Clock/TimeSource (kotlin.time.TimeSource.Monotonic or java.time.Clock) rather than System.currentTimeMillis(); in tests use testScheduler.timeSource or a fake clock advanced alongside the scheduler. currentTime is virtual and unrelated to wall clock.

Real examples. Search-as-you-type (Google Maps, Swiggy search) is tested with virtual time to verify debounce and flatMapLatest cancellation of the stale request.

Analogy. Testing a kitchen timer by spinning its dial rather than waiting for the egg.

Common interview traps.

  • Using System.currentTimeMillis() in production, which virtual time can't control.
  • Off-by-one at the exact boundary (advanceTimeBy is exclusive; use runCurrent).
  • Forgetting to cancel an infinite poller.

notes.title: Cancellation and exceptions in tests
notes.html:
Testing cancellation (Q645). Launch the call, advance until it is mid-way, cancel, advance, and assert cleanup ran and that cancellation propagated.

val job = launch { repo.upload() }
advanceTimeBy(500)
job.cancelAndJoin()
assertTrue(repo.cleanedUp)
assertTrue(job.isCancelled)

Check that the function doesn't swallow CancellationException: its catch (e: Exception) should rethrow; assert no work occurs after cancel (e.g. fake counts calls after cancel).

Exceptions in runTest (Q646).

  • Thrown in the test body: the test fails with it (use assertFailsWith { } or try/catch to assert).
  • In a launch child of the TestScope: it propagates to the test scope and fails the test (reported at the end / on next idle), so you can't catch it with try/catch around launch.
  • async: held until await(); assertFailsWith<X> { deferred.await() }. If never awaited the exception can be lost or reported on cancel depending on parent.
  • backgroundScope: failures there fail the test too in recent versions (confirm in your version); don't rely on it to hide errors.
  • Uncaught exceptions are also reported through TestScope's exception handler; with runTest they are rethrown at the end.

Real examples. Libraries like Retrofit-coroutine adapters and Room's suspend DAOs are tested by cancelling mid-flight to ensure the underlying call/transaction is cancelled.

Analogy. A fire drill: you ring the alarm halfway through the day and check everyone left the building and turned off the stove.

Common interview traps.

  • Wrapping launch in try/catch and expecting to catch its exception.
  • Forgetting to join before asserting cleanup.
  • Testing only the happy cancellation (job cancelled) but not that the CancellationException was rethrown.

notes.title: Flaky tests
notes.html:
Causes and cures (Q648).

Cause Fix
Real Dispatchers.IO/Default in code inject dispatchers, test dispatcher
Thread.sleep / delay in real time virtual time, advanceTimeBy
Mixed schedulers share testScheduler
Forgot resetMain Rule with finished()
Shared mutable state between tests (singletons, static caches) fresh objects per test
Reading .value before work finished advanceUntilIdle() / Turbine
Unconfined vs Standard ordering pick one, document it
StateFlow conflation assertions assert final state / expectMostRecentItem
Real clock / random inject Clock / seeded Random
Leaked coroutines from earlier test use backgroundScope, cancel scopes

Production-style flaky incident (Q647). Symptom: CI fails 1 in 20 runs, only on slow machines. Root cause example: repository used Dispatchers.IO (real) while the test advanced virtual time; on slow runners the IO thread finished after the assertion. Fix: inject the test dispatcher; quarantine; rerun with --rerun-tasks and a stress loop (repeat(100)).

Post-incident (Q657). A hidden race slipped to production because tests ran with Unconfined (everything sequential). Strategy: default to Standard; add a few tests with interleavings (advanceTimeBy between steps); add Turbine "no unexpected events"; run concurrency tests in a stress loop; verify leak detection (runTest fails on unfinished children); add a lint rule banning hard-coded dispatchers.

Real examples. Google's "flaky test" dashboards, Slack and Square engineering posts on eliminating Thread.sleep from test suites.

Analogy. A recipe that depends on the oven's mood: you fix it by controlling the temperature, not by retrying until the cake works.

Common interview traps.

  • "Fixing" flakiness with longer timeouts or retries.
  • Sleeping instead of controlling the scheduler.
  • Letting tests share a singleton scope.

notes.title: Mocks versus fakes and migrating test infrastructure
notes.html:
MockK with suspend and flows (Q649).

coEvery { api.load() } returns Data()           // suspend
coEvery { api.load() } coAnswers { delay(100); Data() }
coEvery { api.load() } throws IOException()
every { dao.observe() } returns flowOf(listOf(item))  // Flow is not suspend: every
coVerify(exactly = 1) { api.load() }

Use coEvery/coVerify for suspend functions and plain every for functions returning Flow. Mockito-kotlin uses whenever (suspend supported in lambdas).

Fake vs mock. A fake is a working light implementation (an in-memory repository holding a MutableStateFlow). Prefer fakes when behavior matters (state over time, flows that emit repeatedly, ordering), and when the contract is stable: tests describe outcomes rather than call sequences, and refactors do not break them. Prefer mocks for interaction checks (was analytics.log called?) and for hard-to-fake systems (a failing IOException at the 3rd call).

Migrating test infrastructure (Q651). Moving from runBlockingTest / TestCoroutineDispatcher (deprecated in kotlinx-coroutines-test 1.6) to runTest: migrate gradually per module; replace TestCoroutineDispatcher with StandardTestDispatcher/UnconfinedTestDispatcher; advanceUntilIdle stays; behavioural difference: eager launch in old dispatcher ran immediately, new ones queue; fix tests that relied on that; run both versions in CI; roll back per module by git revert; track flake rate before/after. Do not migrate test infrastructure and production code in the same PR.

Real examples. Large Android codebases (Square, Slack) migrated in dozens of PRs, module by module, using lint rules to ban deprecated APIs.

Analogy. A mock is an actor following a script and checking you said your lines; a fake is a stunt double that actually does the job on a small scale.

Common interview traps.

  • Using every instead of coEvery for suspend functions.
  • Over-mocking so tests mirror the implementation.
  • Migrating test infra and behavior in the same PR.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• runTest runs on a virtual clock; the 10 s timeout is real time.
  • Use Standard dispatchers by default, share one scheduler, inject dispatchers, and set Main with a rule that resets.
  • advanceTimeBy is exclusive; add runCurrent().
  • Collect stateIn flows in backgroundScope or Turbine; mind conflation and replay-0 subscriptions.
  • Inject clocks and dispatchers for time logic; test cancellation and exceptions explicitly.
  • Kill flakiness at the source (real threads, shared state), not with retries.
  • Prefer fakes for behavior, mocks for interactions; migrate test infra incrementally.

questions.promptHtml: What does runTest do, and why does a test containing delay(10_000) finish in milliseconds?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you understand that coroutine tests do not run on a wall clock. Candidates who have only copy-pasted runTest cannot explain why delay is "free".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "runTest runs the test body in a TestScope whose dispatcher is backed by a TestCoroutineScheduler. That scheduler keeps a virtual clock and a priority queue of tasks ordered by virtual time. When the test body suspends and nothing is runnable at the current virtual time, the scheduler jumps the clock to the next scheduled task instead of sleeping. So delay(10_000) just schedules a task at t+10000 and the clock skips ahead. The test is deterministic and fast, and currentTime tells me how much virtual time passed."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A real dispatcher (Dispatchers.Default) executes a task now, and delay is implemented by a timer thread that resumes the coroutine after real wall-clock time. A test dispatcher replaces both pieces:

  • Dispatching: the task is put into the TestCoroutineScheduler queue instead of a thread pool.
  • delay: TestDispatcher implements Delay, so delay(n) enqueues a resume task at currentTime + n. No timer thread is involved.
virtual time (ms):   0 ---- 1000 ---- 5000 ---- 10000
queue:               [A]    [B]       [C]       [D]
runTest body suspends -> scheduler pops the earliest task, sets currentTime to its time,
runs it, repeats. Real elapsed time ~ 0 ms.

runTest also does these things:

  1. Creates a TestScope (a CoroutineScope with a StandardTestDispatcher and a TestCoroutineScheduler, unless you pass your own).
  2. Runs the body, and when the body returns it keeps advancing until all children of the TestScope finish (it does not wait for backgroundScope).
  3. Applies a timeout (see the timeout question) so a hung test fails instead of blocking CI forever.
  4. Rethrows uncaught exceptions from child coroutines at the end, which makes the test fail.

Since 1.7.0 the runTest / TestScope / TestCoroutineScheduler API is stable. The old runBlockingTest, TestCoroutineDispatcher and TestCoroutineScope were deprecated in 1.6 and are gone in recent versions. Migrate before upgrading.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test
fun delayIsVirtual() = runTest {
    val start = currentTime            // 0
    delay(10_000)
    assertEquals(10_000, currentTime - start)
}

// Broken: runBlocking really waits 10 seconds, and any Dispatchers.Default work is real-time
@Test
fun slow() = runBlocking { delay(10_000) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking virtual time applies to everything. It only applies to coroutines dispatched on the test scheduler. Thread.sleep, withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { delay() } and other real dispatchers use the real clock (see Q650).
  • Using runBlocking in tests "because it works". It works but is slow, and it cannot control ordering.
  • Using System.currentTimeMillis() for assertions. Use currentTime or testScheduler.timeSource.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the dispatcher inside runTest by default? → StandardTestDispatcher. Launched coroutines are queued, not run eagerly.
  2. Does runTest wait for coroutines launched in GlobalScope? → No. They are not children of the TestScope. They run on real dispatchers and leak.
  3. What if a coroutine does CPU work on Dispatchers.Default inside runTest? → It truly runs in parallel on a real thread. runTest only waits for it if the test body awaits it (join/await), and the virtual clock does not model its duration.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE answer says "it skips delays." A senior explains that the skipping comes from a scheduler with a task queue and Delay implemented by the test dispatcher, and states the boundary: only test-scheduler dispatchers get virtual time, so any hard-coded real dispatcher makes the test slow or flaky.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's 4,000-test suite took 11 minutes in CI because repositories hard-coded Dispatchers.IO and used delay(500) inside withContext; after dispatcher injection it dropped to under 2 minutes.

questions.promptHtml: What is the default timeout of runTest, is it virtual or real time, and how do you change it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a version-specific fact that people get wrong, and the virtual vs wall-clock distinction explains many "my test hangs" reports.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "runTest has a whole-test timeout, added in kotlinx.coroutines 1.7.0 with a 10 second default and raised to 60 seconds in 1.8.0. It is measured in real wall-clock time, not virtual time, because its purpose is to stop a genuinely stuck test. I can override it per test with runTest(timeout = 5.seconds). On the JVM the default can also be changed globally with a system property, which I would check in the current docs for the exact name before relying on it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• 1.7.0 introduced runTest(timeout: Duration), default 10 s.
  • 1.8.0 changed the default to 60 s and made it configurable on the JVM (changelog entry #3800). The old dispatchTimeoutMs parameter is deprecated in favour of timeout.
  • The timeout is real time because virtual time is exactly what a stuck test cannot advance: if the test waits for a real thread, a never-completing CompletableDeferred, or a while(true) { yield() } loop, the virtual clock is irrelevant.
  • On timeout you get an exception such as "After waiting for 60s, the test coroutine is not completing", listing the active children. Newer versions help by dumping coroutines on JVM. That list is the first thing to read when debugging.
  • The timeout is not the same as withTimeout inside the code under test. withTimeout(1000) inside the test body is virtual and fires when the scheduler reaches t=1000.
  • Turbine has its own, separate 3 second wall-clock timeout for awaitItem() and friends (see Q642).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test
fun fastFail() = runTest(timeout = 5.seconds) {
    // a hang here fails after 5s of real time, not 60
    neverEmitting.first()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming "60 s" means 60 s of virtual time. A delay(120_000) test passes fine.
  • Raising the timeout to "fix" a hanging test instead of finding the leaked collector (usually an un-cancelled collect on a StateFlow).
  • Quoting 10 s from older blog posts. State the version.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does stateFlow.collect {} inside runTest hang? → StateFlow.collect never completes, so the test coroutine never finishes. Collect in backgroundScope or use first()/Turbine.
  2. Can you set a different timeout for the whole module? → On the JVM there is a system property (check the runTest KDoc for the exact name in your version); otherwise wrap in your own helper that passes timeout.
  3. Why not make the timeout virtual? → Then a stuck test, which never lets the clock advance, would never time out.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer knows "there's a timeout." The senior states 10 s (1.7) vs 60 s (1.8+), real vs virtual, and uses a short explicit timeout on CI-critical suites so hangs fail fast with an actionable message.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hung collect on a StateFlow blocked a CI runner for 60 s on every affected test; dozens of such tests turned a 5 minute pipeline into 40 minutes before anyone looked at the timeout messages.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between StandardTestDispatcher and UnconfinedTestDispatcher, and which would you use by default?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Choosing the wrong one produces tests that either never run the code or hide ordering bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "StandardTestDispatcher queues every dispatched coroutine and runs it only when the scheduler is advanced or the test body suspends, so I control ordering exactly. UnconfinedTestDispatcher starts coroutines eagerly on the calling thread like Dispatchers.Unconfined, but its delay still uses virtual time. runTest defaults to Standard. I default to Standard for the code under test, and use Unconfined mostly to make collectors in backgroundScope subscribe immediately."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
StandardTestDispatcher UnconfinedTestDispatcher
launch {} queued; body does not run yet body runs immediately until first suspension
ordering deterministic, FIFO per virtual time like Unconfined: nested resumption, event-loop style
needs runCurrent() / advanceUntilIdle() yes rarely
delay virtual virtual
hides races no (models a real dispatcher) yes (code runs "too early")

Both share one TestCoroutineScheduler. Constructing without an argument uses the scheduler of Dispatchers.Main if you replaced it with a test dispatcher, else creates a new one. That is why you should pass testScheduler explicitly inside runTest: UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler).

Standard mirrors production because real dispatchers do not run your coroutine before launch returns. Unconfined is a convenience: the state is "already updated" when launch returns, which can mask bugs where real code would see an intermediate state or a different ordering (see Q657).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test
fun standard() = runTest {
    var x = 0
    launch { x = 1 }
    assertEquals(0, x)   // not yet run
    runCurrent()
    assertEquals(1, x)
}

@Test
fun unconfined() = runTest(UnconfinedTestDispatcher()) {
    var x = 0
    launch { x = 1 }
    assertEquals(1, x)   // ran eagerly
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Asserting right after launch with Standard and wondering why nothing happened.
  • Creating UnconfinedTestDispatcher() and runTest with different schedulers, so advanceTimeBy on one does not move the other.
  • Using Unconfined everywhere so tests pass but ordering assumptions are never checked.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When does Standard run the queued work? → When the test body suspends (join, delay, await), or when you call runCurrent/advanceUntilIdle/advanceTimeBy.
  2. Does Unconfined skip delays? → No; delays are still virtual and need the scheduler to advance.
  3. Is Unconfined re-entrant? → It can run resumed continuations nested on the same stack under an event loop rule, so deep chains behave differently from a real dispatcher.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "Unconfined runs immediately." The senior ties each to a purpose: Standard models real asynchrony and finds ordering bugs, Unconfined makes subscription deterministic, and the two must share a scheduler.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A test rule defaulted to Unconfined, so a bug where the UI saw Loading after Success never reproduced in tests but happened on real devices.

questions.promptHtml: How do TestScope, TestCoroutineScheduler, and the dispatchers relate? When two dispatchers in one test must see the same virtual time, how do you ensure it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "My advanceUntilIdle() did nothing" is almost always a scheduler mismatch.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A TestCoroutineScheduler owns the virtual clock and the task queue. A TestDispatcher is just a front-end bound to one scheduler. TestScope holds a scheduler plus a dispatcher. All dispatchers in a test must use the same scheduler, otherwise each has its own clock and advancing one does nothing to the other. Inside runTest I pass testScheduler when creating extra dispatchers, and if I setMain with a test dispatcher, runTest automatically adopts its scheduler."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
TestScope
 ├─ testScheduler : TestCoroutineScheduler  (clock + queue)
 ├─ coroutineContext: StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) + Job + handler
 └─ backgroundScope (cancelled when the test ends)

StandardTestDispatcher(scheduler)  \
UnconfinedTestDispatcher(scheduler) / each is bound to exactly one scheduler

Rules for scheduler selection when you construct a test dispatcher or TestScope without one:

  1. If Dispatchers.Main was replaced with a TestMainDispatcher wrapping a TestDispatcher, use that dispatcher's scheduler.
  2. Otherwise create a fresh scheduler.

So the safest pattern is: set Main first (in a rule), then runTest, then StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) for injected dispatchers. Mismatched schedulers are detected in some paths (an error such as "Detected use of different schedulers" is thrown when a TestScope is given a dispatcher with a different scheduler than its explicit one), but two independent tests dispatchers in a single context often fail silently.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test
fun sameScheduler() = runTest {
    val io = StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)   // shares the clock
    val repo = Repo(ioDispatcher = io)
    val r = async { repo.load() }   // load() uses withContext(io) + delay(1000)
    advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals(1000, currentTime)
    r.await()
}

// Broken: separate scheduler, advanceUntilIdle() does not drive it
val io = StandardTestDispatcher()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• runTest { ... StandardTestDispatcher() ... }: new scheduler (unless Main was set) and a hung or wrong test.
  • Calling Dispatchers.setMain after the dispatcher is created, so they disagree.
  • Believing each TestDispatcher has its own clock "for isolation."

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you get the scheduler in a JUnit rule? → Create TestCoroutineScheduler() in the rule, pass it to the dispatcher, and pass the dispatcher to runTest(dispatcher) or let runTest adopt it via Main.
  2. Can one test have two TestScopes? → Yes, but they should share a scheduler, otherwise virtual times diverge.
  3. What is testScheduler.timeSource? → A TimeSource backed by virtual time (comparable marks since 1.7.0), useful for measuring durations in production code that accepts a TimeSource.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average candidate knows advanceUntilIdle exists. The senior can draw the scheduler/dispatcher/scope relationship and states the selection rule via Main.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shared TestRule created its own UnconfinedTestDispatcher() while tests used runTest() defaults; debounce tests passed individually but not when run after another test that had set Main.

questions.promptHtml: Explain advanceUntilIdle(), advanceTimeBy(), and runCurrent(). What exactly does advanceTimeBy(1000) run, and what does it not run?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Off-by-one at the boundary time is the top cause of failing debounce/timeout tests.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "runCurrent() runs tasks scheduled at the current virtual time and stops. advanceTimeBy(n) moves the clock forward n ms, running tasks scheduled strictly before currentTime + n; tasks exactly at the target time are not run, so I follow it with runCurrent(). advanceUntilIdle() keeps running everything, jumping through all pending delays until the queue is empty. It does not wait for real threads, and it never terminates on an endless periodic coroutine."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• runCurrent(): execute all tasks whose time <= currentTime, including ones those tasks enqueue at the same time. Time does not move.
  • advanceTimeBy(delay): process tasks with time < currentTime + delay, then set the clock to currentTime + delay. The task at exactly the end time is left pending (behaviour since kotlinx.coroutines 1.6). It is intentional so repeated advanceTimeBy slices do not double-execute.
  • advanceUntilIdle(): loop until no tasks remain. With while(true) { delay(1000); poll() } in the scope, it never becomes idle: the test hangs until the timeout. Use advanceTimeBy plus runCurrent, or cancel the loop.
  • All three are extension functions on TestScope that delegate to testScheduler.
t=0 launch { delay(1000); A() }; launch { delay(1001); B() }
advanceTimeBy(1000): A pending (at 1000, not < 1000), B pending, currentTime = 1000
runCurrent():        A runs
advanceTimeBy(1):    clock 1001, B pending at boundary
runCurrent():        B runs

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test
fun boundary() = runTest {
    var done = false
    launch { delay(1000); done = true }
    advanceTimeBy(1000)
    assertFalse(done)       // task at exactly t=1000 not run yet
    runCurrent()
    assertTrue(done)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• advanceTimeBy(300) for debounce(300) and asserting: the emission at exactly t=300 has not run.
  • advanceUntilIdle() with an infinite polling loop or delay loop.
  • Expecting advanceUntilIdle to wait for Dispatchers.IO work.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the boundary task not run? → Design choice to make slicing time deterministic; use runCurrent().
  2. Does advanceUntilIdle move currentTime? → Yes, to the time of the last executed task.
  3. How do you test a polling loop that runs every 5 s for 3 cycles? → advanceTimeBy(15_000 + 1) or advanceTimeBy(15_000); runCurrent(), then cancel the job.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists definitions. The senior states the strict < boundary and what hangs advanceUntilIdle.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flaky "retry after 30 s" test failed whenever refactoring changed the number of tasks queued at t=30000 because the test used advanceTimeBy(30_000) with no runCurrent().

questions.promptHtml: Why do local unit tests of a ViewModel crash with "Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize", and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The standard baseline for any Android coroutine test. Interviewers watch for resetMain and scheduler sharing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "viewModelScope uses Dispatchers.Main.immediate. On the JVM there is no Android main Looper, so the Main dispatcher fails to initialize. kotlinx-coroutines-test provides Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher) to replace it, and resetMain() to restore it. I wrap both in a JUnit TestWatcher rule, MainDispatcherRule, so each test sets Main before and resets it after."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Dispatchers.Main is loaded via ServiceLoader (MainDispatcherFactory). With kotlinx-coroutines-android on a pure JVM test classpath, creating it calls Looper.getMainLooper(), and the stubbed android.jar either throws or returns null, so you get the quoted error: "For tests Dispatchers.setMain from kotlinx-coroutines-test module can be used".
  • setMain(dispatcher) installs a delegating TestMainDispatcher. Everything using Main, including viewModelScope and lifecycleScope in JVM tests, now runs on your test dispatcher.
  • runTest picks up the scheduler from Main if it is a test dispatcher, so the ViewModel and test body share virtual time (Q636).
  • Always call resetMain(). Otherwise Main stays replaced for later tests in the same JVM (Gradle reuses the JVM per module), causing cross-test leakage.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MainDispatcherRule(
    private val dispatcher: TestDispatcher = UnconfinedTestDispatcher()
) : TestWatcher() {
    override fun starting(description: Description) = Dispatchers.setMain(dispatcher)
    override fun finished(description: Description) = Dispatchers.resetMain()
}

class VmTest {
    @get:Rule val main = MainDispatcherRule()

    @Test fun loads() = runTest {
        val vm = ProfileViewModel(FakeRepo())
        advanceUntilIdle()
        assertEquals(Loaded, vm.state.value)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting resetMain().
  • Rule creates its own dispatcher but the test uses runTest(StandardTestDispatcher()): different schedulers.
  • Only setMain in @Before and forgetting classes that create the ViewModel in a field initializer (before the rule runs).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What default dispatcher should the rule use? → Unconfined is Google's sample default and is convenient; Standard is stricter. Make it a constructor param and choose per suite.
  2. Do you need setMain if you inject all dispatchers? → Still yes for viewModelScope and for any library using Main.
  3. Android instrumented tests? → Real Looper exists, so setMain is usually unnecessary there (and can conflict with the real UI thread).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer writes the rule. The senior explains why it fails (ServiceLoader and Looper), why resetMain matters across the JVM, and how Main's scheduler flows into runTest.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Missing resetMain made a later test in the same module read state from the previous test's Main dispatcher, producing failures only when the test order changed.

questions.promptHtml: Why should production classes receive a CoroutineDispatcher instead of referencing Dispatchers.IO directly, and how do you structure it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The single design decision that makes coroutine code testable. Google's Android guidance says to inject dispatchers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Hard-coded dispatchers cannot be replaced in tests, so withContext(Dispatchers.IO) runs on real threads with real time, which is slow and non-deterministic. I inject dispatchers through the constructor with a production default, or use a small DispatcherProvider interface or Hilt qualifiers. In tests I pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) so everything runs on virtual time."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Constructor injection with defaults is lightest: class Repo(private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO).
  • Hilt style: @Qualifier annotation class IoDispatcher plus @Provides @IoDispatcher fun io() = Dispatchers.IO.
  • A DispatcherProvider { main, io, default } bundle is fine for apps with many classes, but avoid a service-locator singleton.
  • Also inject scopes (e.g. an application-level CoroutineScope) rather than GlobalScope, so tests can control and cancel them.
  • Make suspend functions main-safe (withContext(io) inside the repository) so callers do not choose the dispatcher.
  • Inject Clock/TimeSource for wall-clock reads.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class UserRepo(
    private val api: Api,
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO
) {
    suspend fun load(): User = withContext(io) { api.user() }
}

@Test fun load() = runTest {
    val repo = UserRepo(FakeApi(), StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))
    assertEquals(User("a"), repo.load())
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Injecting but then also calling Dispatchers.Default elsewhere (e.g. flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) in an operator chain).
  • Passing UnconfinedTestDispatcher() without the shared scheduler.
  • Injecting a CoroutineScope in tests but never cancelling it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is it OK to use Dispatchers.Unconfined in tests instead of injection? → It removes threads but not real time in delay; and it hides ordering.
  2. Do you inject Dispatchers.Main? → Usually no; setMain handles it, but Dispatchers.Main.immediate references in custom code can be injected too.
  3. Replacing dispatchers via Dispatchers.setMain for IO? → Only Main can be replaced; IO and Default cannot, hence injection.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "so we can mock it." The senior adds main-safety, scope injection, and the audit for stray flowOn(Dispatchers.X) / GlobalScope / Thread.sleep, enforced by a lint or detekt rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A detekt rule banning Dispatchers.IO outside DI modules removed an entire class of flaky tests in one quarter.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate adds a unit test for SearchViewModel. It passes locally in the IDE but you see this on CI for the whole class, and a second problem on one test.

class SearchViewModel(private val repo: SearchRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<UiState>(UiState.Idle)
    val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state

    fun search(q: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.value = UiState.Loading
            _state.value = UiState.Done(repo.search(q))
        }
    }
}

class SearchViewModelTest {
    @Test
    fun search_updatesState() {
        val vm = SearchViewModel(FakeRepo(delayMs = 500))
        vm.search("kotlin")
        assertEquals(UiState.Done(listOf("kotlin")), vm.state.value)
    }
}

CI log: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize. For tests Dispatchers.setMain from kotlinx-coroutines-test module can be used. After a fix by another engineer who added Dispatchers.setMain(StandardTestDispatcher()) (never reset), the test now fails with expected Done but was Idle. 1 in 40 CI runs of unrelated test classes also fails with weird Main behaviour.
questions.promptHtml: Find every problem and fix the test.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add runBlocking" or "add Thread.sleep(600)", which makes it slow and still flaky, or only adding setMain and missing the need to advance the scheduler and reset Main.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is this a local JVM test or instrumented? (Decides whether a Looper exists.) Does FakeRepo use delay or real sleeping? Which version of kotlinx-coroutines-test? (runTest vs old APIs.) Are other test classes calling setMain?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, but to unblock CI I would add the missing MainDispatcherRule.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Main not replaced, hence viewModelScope fails. (b) After setMain(Standard), the launch is queued and never run before the assertion. (c) FakeRepo delay of 500 ms is virtual only if it runs on the test scheduler. (d) Not resetting Main leaks into other classes, the red herring being "unrelated tests flaking".
  4. How I'd verify each: Read the stack trace (ServiceLoader/Looper), run the test with a debugger on vm.state.value after search, check the FakeRepo's implementation, and run the module with --tests ordering shuffled to expose leakage.
  5. Root cause: Three bugs. No Main replacement; no scheduler advancement (the Standard dispatcher queues the launch and the 500 ms virtual delay never elapsed); and setMain without resetMain, so the replaced Main (with a stale scheduler) persists into the next classes in the same Gradle test JVM.
  6. Fix:
class SearchViewModelTest {
    @get:Rule val main = MainDispatcherRule(StandardTestDispatcher())

    @Test fun search_updatesState() = runTest {
        val vm = SearchViewModel(FakeRepo(delayMs = 500))
        vm.search("kotlin")
        assertEquals(UiState.Idle, vm.state.value)   // not run yet
        runCurrent()
        assertEquals(UiState.Loading, vm.state.value)
        advanceTimeBy(501)
        assertEquals(UiState.Done(listOf("kotlin")), vm.state.value)
    }
}

runTest adopts Main's scheduler, so advanceTimeBy drives viewModelScope. 7. Prevention: A single shared MainDispatcherRule in a testFixtures module; a code-review checklist item "no setMain outside the rule"; run tests in random order in nightly CI. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use Thread.sleep (real time, flaky) or runBlocking (does not drive viewModelScope). I would not default to Unconfined just to avoid runCurrent, because then the Loading state is invisible to an assertion that wants to check it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if FakeRepo uses withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { delay(500) }? → The delay is real; inject the dispatcher (see Q650).
  • What if the rule used Unconfined? → Loading would be set and repo.search would suspend immediately in launch, state would be Loading right after search(); the intermediate Idle is never observable.
  • What changes with viewModelScope in Robolectric? → A real main Looper exists, but setMain is still the clean path for virtual time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A module's tests passed alone and failed in the full run because one class set Main in @BeforeClass and never reset it. The scheduler it held was from a finished runTest, so later advanceUntilIdle calls drove a dead clock. Moving everything to one rule with finished { resetMain() } fixed it in an hour; finding it took two days.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests Thread.sleep/runBlocking, misses resetMain.
  • Hire: adds rule, runTest, and advancement; explains why the assertion initially failed.
  • Strong hire: also explains scheduler adoption via Main, the cross-class leak, boundary 501, and the Standard vs Unconfined choice with intermediate state assertions.

questions.promptHtml: A ViewModel exposes uiState built with stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), Loading). How do you test it, and why does vm.uiState.value always return Loading in your first attempt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests understanding of lazily-started sharing, StateFlow never completing, and backgroundScope.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "With WhileSubscribed, the upstream only runs while there is a collector, so reading .value without a subscriber just returns the initial value. In the test I start a collector in backgroundScope using an UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler) and gather emissions into a list. backgroundScope is cancelled automatically at test end and runTest does not wait for it, which matters because StateFlow.collect never completes."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• stateIn(scope, WhileSubscribed, initial) creates the StateFlow immediately with initial, but starts collecting upstream only when subscriptionCount > 0. No subscriber means no upstream work, hence .value == Loading.
  • StateFlow.collect never returns. In a normal launch child of TestScope it keeps runTest waiting until the timeout. backgroundScope (added in 1.7.0) is a scope whose coroutines are cancelled at the end of the test body and are not waited for.
  • The collector should be eager (Unconfined) so it is subscribed before you trigger actions; otherwise the Standard collector is queued, you act, and intermediate values can be conflated away.
  • Conflation: a StateFlow drops intermediate values for slow collectors. With Unconfined the collector is never slow, so you see every distinct value. With Standard it may see only the latest.
  • Timing the stop: after cancelling the collector, advanceTimeBy(5_001) shows upstream stopping, because stopTimeout uses virtual delay.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test
fun uiState_emitsLoadedAfterRepo() = runTest {
    val vm = ProfileViewModel(FakeRepo(user))
    val seen = mutableListOf<UiState>()
    backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) {
        vm.uiState.toList(seen)
    }
    runCurrent()
    assertEquals(listOf(Loading, Loaded(user)), seen)
}

// Broken: no subscriber, upstream never runs
@Test fun broken() = runTest {
    val vm = ProfileViewModel(FakeRepo(user))
    advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals(Loaded(user), vm.uiState.value)   // still Loading
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Collecting with a plain launch and hanging until the 60 s timeout.
  • Using SharingStarted.Eagerly in production to "fix" the test, changing app behaviour for a test's sake. (Better: inject the SharingStarted policy, or collect in the test.)
  • Asserting the full list when conflation or equal-valued states make it nondeterministic. Prefer asserting final value plus key transitions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not first()/take(2).toList()? → Works for terminating cases, but first { it is Loaded } is great when you only care about the end state.
  2. How do you test that upstream stops 5 s after the last subscriber leaves? → Cancel the collector job, advanceTimeBy(5_000) (still active), then advanceTimeBy(1) plus runCurrent() and assert the upstream cancellation flag.
  3. Does backgroundScope swallow exceptions? → No; failures in it still fail the test.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer finds backgroundScope from docs. The senior explains why .value is stale (cold upstream), why Unconfined for the collector but Standard for the code under test, and how conflation limits what the test can promise.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A WhileSubscribed ViewModel had a passing test that only asserted .value after advanceUntilIdle() against the initial Loading state by accident, because the fake's initial value matched.

questions.promptHtml: How does Turbine work, and what are the essential APIs? Why use it instead of toList() in a background coroutine?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Turbine is the de facto library for Flow tests. Interviewers want to see you know its guarantees and its timeout behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "flow.test { ... } collects the flow in a coroutine into an internal channel and gives me a ReceiveTurbine where I pull events in order: awaitItem(), awaitComplete(), awaitError(), expectNoEvents(). It fails if an event was not consumed when the block ends, unless I call cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents(). Compared to a manual list it gives me ordered, suspend-based assertions, a timeout so tests never hang, and the unconsumed-events check. The current stable release is 1.2.x."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• test {} starts collection undispatched, so the flow subscribes immediately and a hot flow emission after test begins is not missed.
  • Events are Item, Complete, Error. They land in an unbounded channel, so order is exact and nothing is conflated by Turbine itself (but the source StateFlow may conflate).
  • On block exit: cancels collection and calls ensureAllEventsConsumed(). A forgotten item fails the test with a message listing it.
  • Timeout: 3 seconds of real wall-clock time per await*, independent of virtual time (README). Overridable with test(timeout = ...) or withTurbineTimeout.
  • expectMostRecentItem() returns the latest and discards earlier ones, handy with StateFlow.
  • testIn(backgroundScope) and turbineScope {} let you test several flows at once.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test
fun counter_emitsThenCompletes() = runTest {
    flow { emit(1); delay(1000); emit(2) }.test {
        assertEquals(1, awaitItem())
        assertEquals(2, awaitItem())   // delay skipped in virtual time
        awaitComplete()
    }
}

@Test
fun viewModel() = runTest {
    vm.state.test {
        assertEquals(Loading, awaitItem())
        vm.refresh()
        assertEquals(Loaded, awaitItem())
        cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents() on an infinite flow with extra events, so the test fails on "unconsumed events."
  • Assuming the 3 s timeout is virtual. A slow CI plus a real Dispatchers.IO call can exceed it.
  • Using awaitItem() expecting an intermediate StateFlow value that was conflated.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you assert nothing was emitted? → expectNoEvents().
  2. How do you test two flows together? → turbineScope { val a = flowA.testIn(backgroundScope); val b = flowB.testIn(backgroundScope); ... }, and end each with cancel()/awaitComplete().
  3. Can Turbine tests run without runTest? → Technically yes, but then you lose virtual time and the timeouts become real waits. Run it inside runTest.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer shows awaitItem. The senior mentions the end-of-block check, the wall-clock timeout vs virtual time, and StateFlow conflation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams adopting Turbine found "silent" tests that previously passed because a toList() coroutine was cancelled before it received the final event.

questions.promptHtml: You test a StateFlow with Turbine and the test either misses states or fails with "Unconsumed events." Explain why, and how do you write assertions that are robust to conflation and ordering?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who used Turbine from those who understand what a StateFlow guarantees.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A StateFlow only guarantees the latest value, and it is equality-conflated, so setting the same value twice emits once, and rapid updates can skip intermediates. Turbine gets exactly what the StateFlow delivers, no more. Replay of the current value means the first awaitItem() is the current state, not the first change. For robust tests I use a dispatcher where collection is eager (Turbine collects undispatched), drive actions with explicit runCurrent(), assert only the transitions the contract promises, and use expectMostRecentItem() or skipItems where intermediate states are not part of the contract."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Turbine's collector is eager, but production code in viewModelScope runs on Main (test dispatcher). With a Standard Main, the ViewModel's launch has not run when you call awaitItem(), but awaitItem() suspends, the scheduler runs queued work, and the item arrives. That works. The mistake is asserting .value between steps without running the scheduler.
  • Conflation: if the ViewModel sets Loading then Loaded in the same dispatched slice, a collector that is dispatched (not eager) sees only Loaded. Turbine itself is eager on the collection side, but the StateFlow slot machinery can still conflate when a value changes twice before the collector resumes. With Unconfined Main, each set resumes the collector immediately, so you see both. With Standard Main, two sets in one task slice produce a conflated Loaded only, depending on whether the collector resumed between. So the test outcome depends on dispatcher choice. Decide which behavior is the contract.
  • Equal values: _state.value = Loaded(x) twice with data class equal values emits once.
  • For SharedFlow(replay=0), events emitted before test {} starts are lost; start Turbine first.
  • Unconsumed events: after awaitItem() of Loaded the VM later emits Idle; the end check fails. Use cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents() or expectNoEvents() deliberately.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test
fun retry_showsLoadingThenData() = runTest {
    vm.state.test {
        assertEquals(Error, awaitItem())          // current value replayed first
        vm.retry()
        assertEquals(Loading, awaitItem())        // contract: Loading visible
        assertEquals(Loaded(data), awaitItem())
        expectNoEvents()
    }
}

// When intermediates are not contract:
vm.state.test {
    vm.retry()
    advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals(Loaded(data), expectMostRecentItem())
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting the initial value not to appear.
  • Writing a test that only passes under Unconfined and calling it a fix for a race.
  • Mixing awaitItem() with advanceUntilIdle() in a way that moves time past a real-time Turbine timeout.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test a one-shot event channel? → receiveAsFlow().test {} before triggering; each event once.
  2. How do you test an error flow? → awaitError() returns the Throwable; assert type and message.
  3. Does Turbine have virtual-time awareness? → Its timeout does not; the runTest virtual clock still advances while it waits because the test coroutine is suspended.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer fights the Unconsumed events error. The senior knows StateFlow semantics (replay-latest, conflation, equality), picks assertions that match the contract, and states the dispatcher dependence explicitly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "flaky" test about a loading spinner was really a contract ambiguity: UI wanted Loading always shown, but the ViewModel could conflate it away on a fast fake; the fix was a minimum-display design, not a test tweak.

questions.contextHtml:
Search-as-you-type for a catalog app (1.2M DAU, p95 query latency 350 ms). Requirement from product: "search after the user pauses typing for 300 ms". The ViewModel:

private val query = MutableStateFlow("")
val results: StateFlow<List<Item>> = query
    .debounce(300)
    .distinctUntilChanged()
    .flatMapLatest { repo.search(it) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())

An engineer wrote this test and it fails: expected 1 call to repo.search but was 0.

@Test fun debounces() = runTest {
    backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.results.collect {} }
    vm.onQuery("k"); advanceTimeBy(100)
    vm.onQuery("ko"); advanceTimeBy(100)
    vm.onQuery("kot"); advanceTimeBy(300)
    assertEquals(1, fakeRepo.callCount)
}

Product also asks: "does it search for the empty string when the user clears the box?" Nobody knows.
questions.promptHtml: Why does this fail, how do you test debounce correctly, and how do you handle the ambiguous requirement?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds Thread.sleep(400) or bumps to advanceTimeBy(1000) without understanding the boundary, and never raises the empty-query question.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should empty input trigger a search or clear results? Is 300 ms measured from the last keystroke (yes for debounce) or a max-wait (sample semantics)? Should repeated identical queries refetch? Is the minimum query length enforced?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A. I'd write the requirement as tests first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Boundary: the third query is emitted at t=200; debounce fires at t=500; advanceTimeBy(300) stops at t=500 without running tasks scheduled exactly at 500. (b) onQuery initial "" was already emitted at t=0 and counted or not counted. (c) The collector in backgroundScope plus WhileSubscribed may start late. (d) Red herring: flatMapLatest is fine here.
  4. How I'd verify each: Print currentTime in the fake repo's search; run with advanceTimeBy(301); check call args list rather than a count.
  5. Root cause: advanceTimeBy(n) excludes tasks at exactly currentTime + n. The debounce timer fires at exactly t=500.
  6. Fix:
@Test fun debounces() = runTest {
    backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.results.collect {} }
    runCurrent()
    fakeRepo.calls.clear()               // ignore the initial "" query
    vm.onQuery("k");   advanceTimeBy(100)
    vm.onQuery("ko");  advanceTimeBy(100)
    vm.onQuery("kot"); advanceTimeBy(300)
    assertTrue(fakeRepo.calls.isEmpty()) // t=500: not fired yet in the < rule
    runCurrent()                         // runs the task at exactly t=500
    assertEquals(listOf("kot"), fakeRepo.calls)
}

And separate tests: pause exactly 299 ms then type again, so no call; empty query behavior per the answer product gives; distinct repeated query is not refetched. 7. Prevention: Make the 300 ms a constructor parameter or constant shared by the test; a test helper advanceTimeByAndRun(ms) doing both steps; put the product decision in the test name. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not shorten the debounce in tests via a hacked config because then the 300 ms contract is untested; I would not assert call counts without asserting arguments.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the repo call takes 350 ms and the user types again mid-call? → flatMapLatest cancels the old call; test by making the fake suspend with delay(350) and verifying the first call observed cancellation.
  • What if product wants "search at most every 300 ms while typing" (throttle)? → That is sample or a custom throttleFirst; the test assertions differ (calls at t=300, 600...).
  • Does debounce get virtual time? → Yes, it uses delay-based timers on the collector's context, so it works under the test scheduler.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team tuned debounce to 150 ms after a "feels slow" review; tests with advanceTimeBy(300) still passed, so the contract change went unnoticed and backend QPS rose 30%. Tests that pin 299/300 boundaries would have flagged it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: real sleeps, or no understanding of the boundary.
  • Hire: finds the advanceTimeBy boundary and fixes with runCurrent/+1.
  • Strong hire: also surfaces the empty-query requirement, tests the negative path (299 ms), arguments over counts, and cancellation of in-flight search.

questions.promptHtml: How do you write a test that proves your suspend function cleans up when cancelled and does not swallow CancellationException?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cancellation is the most-claimed, least-tested coroutine property.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I launch the operation in the test scope, advance to the point it is suspended, call job.cancel(), then runCurrent() and assert on observable cleanup: a finally or invokeOnCompletion flag, a fake's closed state, and job.isCancelled. I also test that the code rethrows CancellationException, for example by catching Exception in the code under test and verifying that the job still ends cancelled, not completed."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Cancellation is cooperative: the coroutine only notices at a suspension point or ensureActive(). So the test needs a suspension point that the fake controls (CompletableDeferred.await(), delay, or suspendCancellableCoroutine).
  • With a Standard dispatcher, cancel does not run the finally until the scheduler runs, so call runCurrent() after cancel().
  • Cleanup that itself suspends must use withContext(NonCancellable); test that by asserting the cleanup finished even though the job was cancelled.
  • To verify the swallow bug: code with try { work() } catch (e: Exception) { log } continues after cancellation; the test asserts that the post-catch code did NOT execute.
  • job.join() completes for cancelled jobs; job.await() on a cancelled Deferred throws CancellationException.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test
fun upload_cleansUpOnCancel() = runTest {
    val gate = CompletableDeferred<Unit>()
    val fake = FakeUploader(gate)               // upload() awaits gate, then returns
    var cleaned = false
    val job = launch {
        try { fake.upload("f") } finally { cleaned = true }
    }
    runCurrent()                                 // reach suspension
    job.cancel()
    runCurrent()
    assertTrue(cleaned)
    assertTrue(job.isCancelled)
}

// Detects swallowing
suspend fun bad() {
    try { delay(1000) } catch (e: Exception) { /* swallowed */ }
    sideEffect()                                  // runs after cancel!
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Asserting before runCurrent().
  • Testing cancellation with withTimeout and a real dispatcher, so timing is wall-clock.
  • Testing only cancellation, not that a thrown CancellationException is not converted into a user-visible error state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test a finally block that suspends? → Use a fake whose cleanup call suspends on a gate and assert it completes only with NonCancellable.
  2. How do you test timeout? → withTimeout inside the code and advanceTimeBy(timeout + 1); assert TimeoutCancellationException is mapped to your domain error.
  3. Detect an un-cooperative CPU loop? → The cancel never takes effect; the test would see isActive still true after runCurrent(); assert with a bounded wait.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer only asserts job.isCancelled. The senior asserts observable cleanup, swallow behavior, NonCancellable cleanup, and cancellation not leaking into error UI state.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cancelled Flow collector in a screen kept a database cursor open because the catch-all catch (e: Exception) swallowed cancellation; a cancellation test would have caught it before a "too many open files" crash.

questions.promptHtml: How do exceptions behave inside runTest? Cover exceptions thrown from the test body, from launch children, from async, and from backgroundScope, and how to assert them.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many tests "pass" while an exception is swallowed, or fail confusingly at the end.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "An exception thrown in the test body fails the test, and I assert expected ones with assertFailsWith. An exception in a launch child propagates through structured concurrency and the TestScope's uncaught-exception handling, failing the test at the end of runTest. For async, it is held until await(), but also cancels the parent unless in a supervisor. For backgroundScope, unhandled exceptions still fail the test. To test a failure path without failing the test, I either catch it where the production code catches it, supply my own CoroutineExceptionHandler, or use a SupervisorJob plus await()/join() and inspect the result."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• TestScope collects unhandled exceptions (since 1.7) and rethrows after the test body completes, even if they occurred in children or the background scope; multiple exceptions are suppressed onto the first.
  • launch { throw X } in a plain TestScope: cancels the scope's job, so sibling coroutines are cancelled and runTest rethrows X. Your test body may see CancellationException instead of X at a later delay.
  • async { throw X }: no crash until await(), then X is thrown; but the parent is cancelled immediately unless a supervisorScope/SupervisorJob is used.
  • To assert the code-under-test's error mapping (Result/UiState.Error), prefer testing the public behavior (state shows Error) over capturing exceptions.
  • When you install a CoroutineExceptionHandler in the context, launch exceptions go to it and do not fail the test; check what it received. Verify that it is invoked only for root coroutines.
  • assertFailsWith<X> { sut.run() } works for suspend calls within runTest as the lambda is suspend-friendly via inline.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test
fun repo_throws_isMappedToError() = runTest {
    val vm = VM(FakeRepo(failWith = IOException("net")))
    vm.state.test {
        skipItems(1)                       // initial
        vm.load()
        assertEquals(UiState.Error("net"), awaitItem())
        cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
    }
}

@Test
fun direct() = runTest {
    val e = assertFailsWith<IllegalStateException> { service.mustBeInitialized() }
    assertEquals("not init", e.message)
}

@Test
fun handler() = runTest {
    val errors = mutableListOf<Throwable>()
    val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) +
        CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, t -> errors += t })
    scope.launch { error("boom") }
    runCurrent()
    assertEquals("boom", errors.single().message)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping launch { throw } in try/catch in the test: it does not catch because the exception travels through the Job hierarchy.
  • Silently swallowing exceptions in a custom scope with a no-op handler so production bugs go green.
  • Believing async exceptions propagate only at await.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why did my test fail with JobCancellationException instead of my exception? → A sibling failed first and cancelled the scope; the root cause is the attached/suppressed exception at the end.
  2. How do you verify an error is reported to Crashlytics? → Inject a reporter fake; assert it received the throwable.
  3. How do you test retry with exponential backoff on failures? → Fake fails N times then succeeds; assert currentTime equals the sum of backoff delays.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer uses assertFailsWith. The senior knows the propagation paths (child/async/background), handler semantics, and tests mapping and reporting rather than raw throws.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A background analytics coroutine threw NullPointerException in tests for months; the test used a swallowing handler, and the bug shipped, crashing 0.4% of sessions.

questions.contextHtml:
Android monorepo, 3,800 unit tests, CI on 8 parallel Gradle workers. Over two weeks the pipeline went from 2% to 14% red builds; re-run goes green 9 times out of 10. Merge queue is backing up (median time-to-merge 25 min to 70 min). Failures are spread over about 60 different tests, mostly ViewModel and repository tests, with messages like:

AssertionError: expected:<Loaded> but was:<Loading>
kotlinx.coroutines.test.UncompletedCoroutinesError: After waiting for 60s, the test coroutine is not completing
IllegalStateException: This job has not completed yet

Changes in those two weeks: Kotlin and coroutines upgrade (1.7 to 1.9), a new shared MainDispatcherRule, 25 new tests by a new team, and Gradle maxParallelForks raised from 2 to 4. Failures cluster on CI and almost never reproduce on laptops.
questions.promptHtml: You are tech lead. How do you stop the bleeding and find the root cause?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retries to CI" or "increase timeouts," which hides the signal, plus blaming the coroutines upgrade without evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do the flaky tests share a module or a base class? (Shared state.) Is it the same tests failing or random ones? (Order dependence vs inherent nondeterminism.) Does failure rate correlate with maxParallelForks? Do failing tests use real dispatchers anywhere?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Quarantine the top 10 offenders behind a @Flaky tag that runs in a non-blocking job with a ticket per test; allow one automatic retry only on the quarantined job, and keep the main job strict. Revert maxParallelForks to 2 as a diagnostic.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Real dispatchers or real time in tests (Dispatchers.IO/Default, Thread.sleep, wall-clock timeouts, Turbine's 3 s real timeout) that break under load with 4 forks on a shared runner. (b) Shared global state across tests in one JVM: Dispatchers.setMain not reset, singletons, static caches, scopes not cancelled. (c) Test-order dependence introduced by the new rule. (d) Behaviour changes in the coroutines upgrade, e.g. a changed default timeout (10 s to 60 s in 1.8) or TestScope exception reporting that surfaces previously hidden failures. (e) Red herring: CPU contention alone, since it only exposes (a).
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the failing classes with --tests repeated 200 times under taskset-limited CPU; run in random and reverse order; grep for Dispatchers.(IO|Default), Thread.sleep, GlobalScope, runBlocking in the failing modules; add a rule that asserts Dispatchers.Main is restored (finished callback) and that no non-test coroutine threads (DefaultDispatcher-worker-*) exist after a test; collect Gradle test reports per failure signature.
  5. Root cause (typical composite): The new MainDispatcherRule created UnconfinedTestDispatcher() with its own scheduler while tests used runTest with a different one in some classes; one base class called setMain in @BeforeClass and never reset, so a later class inherited a dead scheduler. Separately, repositories used withContext(Dispatchers.IO); with 4 forks, the real thread work exceeded Turbine's 3 s wall-clock timeout and advanceUntilIdle ran before real work finished.
  6. Fix: Short term: single rule, finished { resetMain() }, delete per-class setMain; use runTest with scheduler adopted from Main. Long term: inject all dispatchers (Q639), ban Dispatchers.IO outside DI via detekt, a base CoroutineTestRule that fails if the Default/IO pool was touched.
class CoroutineTestRule(val dispatcher: TestDispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher()) : TestWatcher() {
    override fun starting(d: Description) = Dispatchers.setMain(dispatcher)
    override fun finished(d: Description) = Dispatchers.resetMain()
}
  1. Prevention: Run a nightly job that repeats every test 20 times in random order and reports flake rate per test; fail new tests that sleep or use real dispatchers via lint; a dashboard of flake rate with an owner per module.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not blanket-retry the main job, or raise timeouts to 5 minutes (turns a 60 s failure into a 5 min blocked runner and keeps the bug). I would not revert the coroutines upgrade without proof; that loses the exception reporting that revealed real bugs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if failures only occur on one Mac runner? → Check JDK/thread limits and file system timing; real-time code is at fault, so removing real time from the tests makes the runner irrelevant.
  • What if the flaky test is a Room test? → Room uses its own executors (query executor); use an in-memory db with setQueryExecutor(testExecutor) or the test dispatcher via setQueryCoroutineContext.
  • How do you prove a fix? → 500 iterations in random order with CPU pinned; 0 failures.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "random" 8% failure rate traced to one test that left a never-ending SharedFlow collector on a leaked application-scope; the collector's Dispatchers.Default thread raced with the next test's fakes. A guard rule listing live threads named DefaultDispatcher-worker after each test made the culprit obvious in one run.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries/timeouts as the fix; no hypotheses.
  • Hire: identifies real dispatchers/time and Main leakage; proposes reproducible verification.
  • Strong hire: quarantine strategy, thread-leak guard, changelog-aware reasoning (60 s default timeout, exception reporting), and prevention through lint and flake dashboards.

questions.promptHtml: List the main causes of flaky coroutine tests and how you eliminate each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors are expected to own test reliability. The answer should be a taxonomy, not anecdotes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Flakiness comes from letting anything nondeterministic into the test: real dispatchers and threads, real time (Thread.sleep, wall-clock timeouts), shared state between tests (unreset Main, singletons, leaked scopes), uncontrolled ordering (Unconfined hiding races, or Standard without advancing), and unbounded waits. The cure is to put every coroutine on one test scheduler, inject dispatchers and clocks, reset global state, and make every wait explicit and bounded."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cause Symptom Fix
Hard-coded Dispatchers.IO/Default passes alone, fails under CPU load inject dispatcher; use test scheduler
delay inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO) slow test, real time inject dispatcher (Q650)
Thread.sleep / real withTimeout timing-sensitive virtual time, advanceTimeBy
Missing resetMain fails depending on order MainDispatcherRule
Mismatched schedulers advanceUntilIdle ineffective share testScheduler
Leaked coroutines / GlobalScope next test sees stray work inject scope; backgroundScope; cancel in teardown
Turbine 3 s wall timeout under load intermittent timeouts remove real work; raise timeout only for known real-IO tests
Unconfined hiding race passes in test, fails in prod use Standard for code under test
Assertions on conflated StateFlow intermediates off-by-one states assert contract, not accidents
Static singletons (DI graph, caches) state bleed reset or construct per test
Real I/O (network, disk, Room defaults) env-dependent fakes, in-memory db with test executor

Detection: run tests in random/reverse order, repeat N times, run with CPU throttling, add thread-leak assertion.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Flaky: real time and real thread
@Test fun flaky() = runBlocking {
    repo.refresh()                // withContext(Dispatchers.IO)
    delay(200)                    // hoping IO finished
    assertTrue(repo.fresh)
}
// Deterministic
@Test fun stable() = runTest {
    val repo = Repo(io = StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))
    repo.refresh()
    assertTrue(repo.fresh)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
