• "Fixing" by making the delay longer.
  • Blaming CI hardware.
  • Marking a test @Ignore rather than finding which of the above applies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you detect leaked coroutines? → Use TestScope and let runTest fail with UncompletedCoroutinesError; for app scopes inject and cancel, and check thread names after tests.
  2. Is runBlocking itself a flakiness source? → It is deterministic for sequential code, but does not provide virtual time and uses real time.
  3. Why can Unconfined produce flakiness? → Order depends on resumption nesting and thread of the caller if non-test dispatchers are mixed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "avoid sleep." The senior produces the taxonomy, the detection tools (random order, repeat, thread guard), and the policy for the team (flake budget, quarantine).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One team measured that 70% of its flakes came from only two causes, hard-coded Dispatchers.IO and un-reset Main, and removed them with one lint rule and one shared rule.

questions.promptHtml: How do you stub suspend functions and flows with MockK, and when would you prefer a hand-written fake over a mock?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Test design maturity. Mock-heavy tests are brittle, and coroutines add traps (suspension, time, flows).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "With MockK I use coEvery { repo.get(1) } returns x to stub suspend functions and coVerify to check calls; for flows I return flowOf(...) or a MutableSharedFlow I control. coAnswers { delay(100); x } lets a stub suspend in virtual time. I prefer fakes for repositories and data sources: they hold real state, behave consistently across tests, and test behavior rather than call sequences. I use mocks for interaction boundaries I only need to verify, such as an analytics logger or a one-way command."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• every/verify are for non-suspend; use coEvery/coVerify/coAnswers for suspend calls. Calling a suspend function inside plain every fails to compile (it requires a coroutine context).
  • Throwing: coEvery { repo.get(1) } throws IOException().
  • Suspending stub: coEvery { repo.get(1) } coAnswers { delay(500); user } runs on the caller's dispatcher, so delay is virtual if the caller is in runTest.
  • Flow stubs: every { repo.observe() } returns flow (no co needed, since observe() is not suspend).
  • Sequenced results: returnsMany, or coAnswers with counters.
  • coVerifyOrder, coVerify(exactly = 1), confirmVerified guard unexpected calls.
  • Mock drawbacks: tests encode implementation (call order and counts), refactors break tests without behaviour change, relaxed = true hides unstubbed calls, and stateful interactions (insert then observe) need hand-built answers.
  • Fakes: class FakeUserRepo : UserRepo { private val users = MutableStateFlow(listOf<User>()); var failNext = false; override fun observe() = users; override suspend fun add(u: User) { if (failNext) throw IOException(); users.value += u } }. A fake can also hold gates (CompletableDeferred) to control suspension and timing.
  • Mockito-Kotlin equivalent: whenever(repo.get(1)).thenReturn(x) inside a suspend context.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test
fun load_error() = runTest {
    val repo = mockk<UserRepo>()
    coEvery { repo.get(1) } throws IOException("net")
    val vm = ProfileVM(repo)
    vm.load(1); runCurrent()
    assertEquals(UiState.Error("net"), vm.state.value)
    coVerify(exactly = 1) { repo.get(1) }
}

// Fake with a gate to test the in-flight state
class FakeRepo : UserRepo {
    val gate = CompletableDeferred<User>()
    override suspend fun get(id: Int) = gate.await()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• relaxed = true returning a fake Unit/null for a suspend call so the test never exercises the intended path.
  • Verifying call counts on a retry loop and accidentally pinning the number of retries.
  • Mocking Flow types with mockk<Flow<T>>() instead of returning a real flow.
  • MockK on final classes works (inline mock maker), but mocking static/top-level suspend functions requires mockkStatic, which is global and must be unmocked.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is coEvery needed? → The stubbed function is suspend; coEvery provides a coroutine context for the recording.
  2. How does a fake help test in-flight loading states? → Return a CompletableDeferred you complete later.
  3. When would you accept mocks for repositories? → Thin delegations or a boundary with no meaningful state, or when writing a fake costs more than it saves.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer demonstrates syntax. The senior states a policy: fakes for state-holding collaborators, mocks for pure interaction verification, and avoids over-specification of internal calls.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A large refactor of a repository's internals broke 300 mock-based tests though behavior was unchanged; the team replaced mocks with a handful of fakes and later refactors touched almost no tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A test for a token-refresh component takes 3.2 seconds locally and passes; on CI, with shared CPUs, it sometimes fails with a Turbine timeout. The author insists "it uses runTest, so delays are virtual."

class TokenRefresher(private val api: AuthApi) {
    suspend fun refreshWithBackoff(): Token = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        var wait = 500L
        repeat(3) {
            try { return@withContext api.refresh() }
            catch (e: IOException) { delay(wait); wait *= 2 }
        }
        api.refresh()
    }
}

@Test
fun retriesThenSucceeds() = runTest {
    val api = FakeApi(failures = 3)
    val t = TokenRefresher(api).refreshWithBackoff()
    assertEquals("tok", t.value)
    assertEquals(3500, currentTime)
}

Observed: the final assertion fails with expected:<3500> but was:<0> when the author removes a leftover Thread.sleep, and the test visibly takes 3.5 s of real time.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Delays are always skipped in runTest, so the clock is wrong" or removing the assertion.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where does Dispatchers.IO get chosen: constructor or hard-coded? Is there a retry cap and jitter requirement? Is this used in an OkHttp authenticator (blocking context)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; ensure CI is not blocked by raising nothing, and instead fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) withContext(Dispatchers.IO) switches to a real dispatcher, so delay there uses the real clock (the test dispatcher no longer ran it). (b) The author's Thread.sleep was masking it. (c) Red herring: repeat or return@withContext.
  4. How I'd verify: Print Thread.currentThread().name inside the delay: DefaultDispatcher-worker-N. Check currentTime stays 0 while wall time is 3.5 s.
  5. Root cause: Virtual time exists only for coroutines running on a TestDispatcher of the test scheduler. withContext(Dispatchers.IO) moves the continuation to a real thread pool whose delay is implemented by the real default delay (timer). currentTime therefore stays 0 and the test pays full wall time, and under load blows through Turbine/runTest timeouts.
  6. Fix:
class TokenRefresher(
    private val api: AuthApi,
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO
) {
    suspend fun refreshWithBackoff(): Token = withContext(io) { /* same */ }
}

@Test fun retriesThenSucceeds() = runTest {
    val r = TokenRefresher(FakeApi(failures = 3), StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))
    val t = r.refreshWithBackoff()
    assertEquals("tok", t.value)
    assertEquals(500 + 1000 + 2000, currentTime)   // 3500 virtual ms
}

Also, the backoff delay does not need to be on IO at all; only blocking calls do. Better to move delay outside withContext(io) and keep IO scoped around api.refresh() if it blocks. 7. Prevention: Detekt rule banning Dispatchers.IO literals outside DI; code-review rule "no delay inside withContext(IO)". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use UnconfinedTestDispatcher as a workaround (still need injection), and I would not shorten the backoff via a test flag since that removes the 500/1000/2000 contract.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if api.refresh() is a blocking OkHttp call? → The fake is not blocking; production still needs IO for the real call, which is why the dispatcher is injected, not removed.
  • What if the 4th failure must propagate? → Test with failures = 4 and assertFailsWith, asserting currentTime == 3500 before the throw.
  • Should the delay add jitter? → Then inject a Random seeded in tests.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A suite was "fast" until someone logged currentTime and found it was 0 in every test: a tenth of the suite spent real seconds in IO-bound delays, adding up to 4 minutes per CI run.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot explain why currentTime is 0.
  • Hire: identifies the real dispatcher switch and injects it.
  • Strong hire: also restructures so only blocking calls use IO, asserts the exact backoff sum, and adds prevention (lint, seeded jitter).

questions.contextHtml: Monolith Android app, 14 feature modules, 2,300 coroutine tests. The suite uses runBlockingTest, TestCoroutineDispatcher, and TestCoroutineScope (deprecated in kotlinx-coroutines-test 1.6). Platform wants to upgrade to coroutines 1.9 and Kotlin 2.x this quarter, which requires removing those APIs (they are removed in recent versions). Main branch merges about 120 PRs per week; feature teams cannot freeze. 15% of tests use TestCoroutineDispatcher directly through a shared CoroutineRule. Some tests rely on the old eager-by-default behaviour (TestCoroutineDispatcher ran launches immediately).
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration so that CI stays green and no feature team is blocked.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Find-and-replace runBlockingTest with runTest and fix failures," which breaks hundreds of tests at once and blocks merges.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tests assume eager execution? Is the shared rule used across modules or private? Do any tests use pauseDispatcher/resumeDispatcher/advanceTimeBy semantics from the old API? Is there a deadline tied to a Kotlin upgrade?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze new usage: lint/detekt rule banning runBlockingTest and TestCoroutineDispatcher in new code and PR checks, while old tests still compile.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (a) Eager vs queued semantics: old TestCoroutineDispatcher was eager; runTest default is Standard, so tests assert too early. (b) Exceptions: the old API failed differently on uncaught exceptions; runTest reports them at the end, exposing hidden failures. (c) Timeouts: runTest times out on hung tests; old API had dispatchTimeoutMs. (d) Scheduler mismatch between the rule and tests.
  4. How I'd verify: Migrate one module as a pilot on a branch; run each migrated test 50 times; compare pass/fail before and after; review any test that needed advanceUntilIdle additions for real ordering bugs.
  5. Root cause of the difficulty: Semantics changed, not just names; a mechanical rename cannot preserve eager behaviour.
  6. Fix (plan):
    • Step 1: introduce a new MainDispatcherRule built on StandardTestDispatcher/UnconfinedTestDispatcher with the same public shape as the old rule, so tests keep compiling.
    • Step 2: provide migration shims in a test-utils module: fun runTestEager(block) = runTest(UnconfinedTestDispatcher()) { block() } to preserve old eager semantics at call sites that need it (as a temporary, tracked shortcut).
    • Step 3: codemod runBlockingTest { } to runTest { } per module, owned by that module's team via a tracking issue and CI dashboard; run codemod PRs in small batches (one module per PR).
    • Step 4: remove shims when the dashboard hits 0; then upgrade the coroutines version.
// before
@Test fun t() = runBlockingTest { vm.load(); assertEquals(Loaded, vm.state.value) }
// after (explicit, no eagerness assumed)
@Test fun t() = runTest { vm.load(); runCurrent(); assertEquals(Loaded, vm.state.value) }
  1. Prevention: Keep the lint rule permanently; document test conventions; add a "tests must be deterministic under Standard dispatcher" guideline; periodic dependency update cadence to avoid a large jump.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not do one 2,300-test PR; I would not upgrade the library first and fix breakage afterwards; I would not convert everything to Unconfined permanently, since that hides ordering bugs, though it is acceptable as a temporary, tracked shim.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if a module cannot migrate before the deadline? → Keep it on a pinned, isolated test source set only if compile compatibility exists; otherwise rewrite the few remaining tests; deprecation APIs cannot coexist with the removed versions.
  • How do you measure progress? → Count occurrences of banned APIs per module in CI and chart weekly.
  • What do you do with tests that start failing after conversion to Standard? → Treat as potential real races; fix the test, or the code if it relied on eager timing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration surfaced 11 tests that were passing only because an exception in a child coroutine was silently dropped by the old scope. Two of them pointed at real production crashes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: global find-and-replace.
  • Hire: staged by module, shim and lint, understands eager vs Standard.
  • Strong hire: risk list (exceptions, timeouts, schedulers), dashboard-driven ownership, temporary shim with removal date, and treats newly failing tests as signal.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what runTest does internally from start to finish, including how it decides when the test is done, what it does with leaked coroutines, and how real asynchronous work interacts with the virtual clock.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A staff-level check of whether you can reason about test hangs and UncompletedCoroutinesError instead of trial and error.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "runTest builds a TestScope, starts the body as a child coroutine on the test dispatcher, and then loops on the real thread: it runs the scheduler (executing queued tasks and jumping virtual time) until the body is done and no work remains, and if the scheduler is idle but the body is not complete, it waits in real time for external completion such as a real-thread coroutine finishing, up to the timeout. At the end it cancels backgroundScope, fails if non-background children are still running, and rethrows collected uncaught exceptions."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rough sequence (names are conceptual; the exact implementation varies by version):

1. create/adopt TestScope: testScheduler + StandardTestDispatcher (or one adopted from Main)
2. launch body as a coroutine in that scope
3. loop:
     scheduler.tryRunNextTaskUnless { body done and nothing else }  // virtual time jumps happen here
     if no task is ready and body incomplete:
         wait (real time) for an external event, such as a Dispatchers.IO coroutine resuming,
         because only that can enqueue more test tasks
     if real time since start > timeout -> fail with UncompletedCoroutinesError
4. body finished -> drain: advance until idle so children delayed work completes
5. cancel backgroundScope and wait for it to finish
6. if TestScope still has active children -> UncompletedCoroutinesError
7. rethrow uncaught exceptions collected during the test (first one with suppressed others)

Consequences:

  • Virtual time jumps only when the test thread has nothing ready to run. Work on real threads makes the loop wait in real time.
  • A coroutine blocked on a never-completing deferred with nothing scheduled keeps the loop waiting until the timeout. This is the typical hang.
  • A while(true) { delay(x) } loop in a normal child keeps the scheduler non-idle forever (always another task), so runTest never finishes; in backgroundScope it is ignored and cancelled at the end.
  • advanceUntilIdle() inside the body is just a manual version of the loop's step 3.
  • Because the scheduler runs on the thread executing runTest (JVM), tests are mostly single-threaded unless you introduce real dispatchers.
  • JS/Native differences: on JS runTest returns a Promise and has no thread to block. Not relevant for Android JVM tests but relevant to KMP.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// hangs until timeout: child never ends
@Test fun hang() = runTest {
    launch { while (true) { delay(1000) } }       // keeps scheduler busy forever
}
// fixed
@Test fun ok() = runTest {
    backgroundScope.launch { while (true) { delay(1000); tick() } }
    advanceTimeBy(3_001); runCurrent()
    assertEquals(3, ticks)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking runTest is "runBlocking with virtual time" in every respect; leaked non-background children fail it.
  • Putting awaitCancellation() or an infinite collector in the main scope.
  • Expecting runTest to wait for GlobalScope.launch.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does runTest not fail immediately on a leaked child? → It first lets the scheduler drain; a child that eventually finishes is fine; only never-ending ones hit the timeout.
  2. How does runTest interact with Dispatchers.Main replaced? → It adopts the Main test dispatcher's scheduler so the code under test and the body share a clock.
  3. What differs between runTest and TestScope.runTest? → runTest on a TestScope reuses that scope (useful for sharing a scope across a test class setup); the scope can only be used once.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average candidate knows virtual time. The senior can narrate the loop, the real-time wait for external completion, the drain-then-check rule, and apply it to diagnose a hang.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Understanding the drain rule let a team diagnose a test that timed out only when a retry loop was added: the loop's perpetual delay kept the scheduler non-idle.

questions.contextHtml:
CI nightly shows 23 tests failing with:

kotlinx.coroutines.test.UncompletedCoroutinesError:
After waiting for 1m, the test coroutine is not completing, there were active child jobs:
[StandaloneCoroutine{Active}@3f2a, StateFlowImpl collect ...]

Each failing test blocks a runner for the full 60 s; the suite grew from 6 min to 31 min. All failing tests are ViewModel tests for screens that recently moved from LiveData to StateFlow with stateIn(..., WhileSubscribed(5_000), ...). The same tests passed with LiveData. There are 340 other ViewModel tests that are fine. Reviewer comments suggest "just bump the timeout".
questions.promptHtml: What's going on, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Bump the timeout or add @Ignore; or blames StateFlow being "broken in tests".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do the failing tests call collect inside runTest directly? Do the 340 passing tests use Turbine or first()? Is the stuck child StateFlow collect the test's own collector? Did the timeout drop (timeout param) or is 60 s the default (1.8+)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set runTest(timeout = 5.seconds) in the shared test helper (or the JVM system property) so hangs fail fast and CI time recovers; do not ignore the tests.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Tests collect a StateFlow in the TestScope (via launch { vm.state.collect { } } or .toList()), which never completes. (b) The ViewModel's stateIn(viewModelScope) coroutine is a child of the Main dispatcher scope, not the TestScope; it is fine. (c) A custom while(true) polling in the VM keeps the scheduler busy. (d) Red herring: LiveData tests passed because observeForever doesn't block runTest.
  4. How I'd verify: Read the active child jobs list, which names StateFlowImpl collect; grep the failing tests for collect/toList outside backgroundScope; run one with the IDE coroutine debugger or DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() to see where it is suspended.
  5. Root cause: StateFlow.collect is a never-ending suspension. In LiveData tests observeForever returned immediately. In the migrated tests a plain launch { collect } child of the TestScope stays active forever, so runTest waits for it until the timeout.
  6. Fix: Put collectors in backgroundScope, or switch to Turbine/first {}.
@Test fun loads() = runTest {
    val values = mutableListOf<UiState>()
    backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.state.toList(values) }
    vm.load(); runCurrent()
    assertEquals(Loaded, values.last())
}

Add a helper fun <T> TestScope.collectIn(flow: Flow<T>): List<T> that wraps this pattern. 7. Prevention: Template for ViewModel tests; Turbine in the style guide; short global timeout; a detekt rule flagging .collect { directly inside runTest with a StateFlow-typed receiver is hard, so use review checklist plus the short timeout. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not bumping timeouts. Not making the ViewModel SharingStarted.Eagerly for tests (changes production behavior). Not @Ignore.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the hang is from the VM polling every 5 s? → Inject a poll interval/scope or make the ticker cancel with the subscribers; assert via advanceTimeBy.
  • What if the tests run on JS/Native KMP? → runTest returns a Promise; same logic, timeouts apply.
  • What if an awaitCancellation() shows as active? → Run it under backgroundScope, or cancel the owning job.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A full-suite time doubled with no failing assertions; the cause was 40 tests quietly hitting a 60 s timeout, each "passing" because the exception was caught by a test wrapper. A 5 s global timeout turned a silent slowdown into an immediate red build.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises timeout, ignores tests.
  • Hire: identifies the never-completing StateFlow collect and uses backgroundScope or Turbine.
  • Strong hire: reads the active-jobs message, shortens the global timeout, explains LiveData vs StateFlow difference, and provides a shared helper and review guidance.

questions.contextHtml:
A checkout ViewModel emits one-shot navigation events through a MutableSharedFlow (replay = 0, no extra buffer). The test is green locally, but a second test for "payment failed" is red on every run and a third passes only on some machines.

class CheckoutViewModel(private val pay: PayUseCase) : ViewModel() {
    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<Event>()
    val events: SharedFlow<Event> = _events

    fun onPayClicked() = viewModelScope.launch {
        _events.emit(if (pay()) Event.GoToReceipt else Event.ShowError)
    }
}

class CheckoutTest {
    @get:Rule val main = MainDispatcherRule(UnconfinedTestDispatcher())

    @Test fun success() = runTest {
        val vm = CheckoutViewModel(FakePay(ok = true))
        vm.onPayClicked()
        assertEquals(Event.GoToReceipt, vm.events.first())   // test 1
    }

    @Test fun failure() = runTest {
        val vm = CheckoutViewModel(FakePay(ok = false))
        vm.onPayClicked()
        assertEquals(Event.ShowError, vm.events.first())     // test 2
    }
}

Test 2 times out; 50k DAU feature, and QA reports the receipt screen sometimes opens twice on slow devices. The team asks whether the test or the code is wrong.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why these tests behave this way, fix the tests, and say whether the production code has a bug.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Switching to replay = 1 to make the test pass, which changes production semantics (events replay to new collectors, so the receipt screen re-opens on rotation).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the event meant to be delivered exactly once, even if the UI is not collecting at that instant? What is the UI collection policy (repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED))? Are events allowed to be dropped when the screen is in the background?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not a test-only issue; the "receipt opens twice" report suggests a production bug, so I'd raise it as a separate ticket first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The tests emit before subscribing. With replay = 0 and no subscribers, emit returns immediately and the value is lost; first() subscribes after the event was dropped, so it hangs. (b) Test 1 passes by accident because FakePay suspends and the Unconfined first() subscribes first in some orderings. (c) In production, SharedFlow with no buffer drops events when there are no collectors (during rotation/background), and duplicates arise if a UI re-collects with a replay or the click fires twice. (d) Red herring: dispatcher choice per se.
  4. How I'd verify: Make FakePay suspend on a gate to show order-dependence; add a Turbine test that subscribes first; reproduce in a UI test with rotation at the moment of the event; log subscriptionCount in emit.
  5. Root cause: A hot SharedFlow with replay = 0 delivers only to current subscribers. The test subscribes after onPayClicked() already completed under Unconfined Main, which is exactly the lost-event case. The test is wrong in ordering, but the code reveals a real design weakness: events can be lost when nobody is collecting, and are not guaranteed exactly-once.
  6. Fix (tests):
@Test fun failure() = runTest {
    val vm = CheckoutViewModel(FakePay(ok = false))
    vm.events.test {                       // subscribe first
        vm.onPayClicked()
        assertEquals(Event.ShowError, awaitItem())
        cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
    }
}

Fix (code): see the one-off events section for the options; a common choice is a Channel<Event>(Channel.BUFFERED) exposed via receiveAsFlow() (each event consumed once, buffered while the UI is away), or model the event as state that the UI acknowledges (state.navigation plus onNavigated()), and make onPayClicked idempotent while a payment is in flight. 7. Prevention: A ViewModel test template that starts Turbine before actions; a test that simulates "no collector at emit time" and asserts the chosen semantics; double-click protection tested with two calls. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not replay = 1 for events. Not extraBufferCapacity with DROP_OLDEST for navigation (silent loss). A Channel can still drop on cancellation of the collector mid-delivery, so state-based events are the safest for critical navigation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did test 1 pass? → The fake returned without suspending, and ordering under Unconfined plus first() happened to subscribe before the emit; relying on it is accidental.
  • Would Standard Main change things? → launch would be queued, so first() could subscribe before the emit runs, and the test would pass more reliably; but the right fix is explicit subscribe-first.
  • How would you test "event buffered while UI away"? → With a Channel-backed flow: call the action, then events.test { awaitItem() } afterwards and assert delivery.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payment confirmation event vanished for about 0.3% of users who rotated at the exact moment of delivery; the unit tests were green because they subscribed late in a way that happened to work.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: changes the code to make the test pass without analysis.
  • Hire: explains lost event with replay=0 and subscribes first with Turbine.
  • Strong hire: separates test bug from design weakness, proposes Channel or state-based events, adds a "no collector" test and idempotency.

questions.contextHtml:
A team's tests all use UnconfinedTestDispatcher because "Standard needs advanceUntilIdle everywhere." A spinner bug shipped: on a 3G network the screen flashes Loaded(empty) for one frame before Loaded(data). The ViewModel:

val state: StateFlow<UiState> = combine(userFlow, ordersFlow) { u, o -> UiState.Loaded(u, o) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState.Loading)

userFlow emits at 40 ms, ordersFlow at 900 ms from a slow API; combine on a Room-backed ordersFlow first emits emptyList() immediately. The existing test:

@Test fun loads() = runTest(UnconfinedTestDispatcher()) {
    val vm = VM(FakeUser(user), FakeOrders(orders))   // both fakes emit synchronously
    assertEquals(UiState.Loaded(user, orders), vm.state.value)
}

It passes. Release candidate has 12k crash-free sessions and 4% of QA runs see the flash.
questions.promptHtml: Why did the test not catch it, and how would you restructure the tests and dispatcher strategy?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a delay to the fake" without changing the dispatcher or the assertions, or "the UI team should debounce it."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the intermediate Loaded(user, empty) state a legitimate product state, or should the UI show a spinner until orders load? Does Room's initial empty list mean "loading" or "no orders"? What is the minimum acceptable sequence of states?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a guard in the ViewModel: represent orders as Result/Loading so combine cannot produce Loaded with unloaded orders.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The fakes are synchronous and the dispatcher is eager, so the only observable state is the final one; the intermediate is never exercised. (b) Real flows emit at different times, so combine publishes a partial result. (c) The test asserts .value once, never the sequence. (d) Red herring: network speed itself.
  4. How I'd verify: Rewrite the fakes to emit on gates or with delays (delay(900)), run with Turbine, and observe the sequence Loading, Loaded(user, []), Loaded(user, orders).
  5. Root cause: Test infrastructure erased time. Unconfined plus synchronous fakes collapse a multi-step async sequence to its final value, so sequence bugs and races are untestable. The production bug is a modeling issue: using an empty list as both "unloaded" and "loaded empty".
  6. Fix:
class VMTest {
    @get:Rule val main = MainDispatcherRule(StandardTestDispatcher())

    @Test fun neverShowsLoadedBeforeOrdersArrive() = runTest {
        val user = flow { delay(40); emit(u) }
        val orders = flow { delay(900); emit(listOf(o)) }
        val vm = VM(user, orders)
        vm.state.test {
            assertEquals(UiState.Loading, awaitItem())
            assertEquals(UiState.Loaded(u, listOf(o)), awaitItem())   // no partial state
            cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
        }
        assertEquals(900, currentTime)
    }
}

Production: model orders as Loadable<List<Order>> and map combine to Loading until both are loaded. 7. Prevention: Policy: tests for async state machines use Standard and time-shaped fakes; Unconfined is allowed only for collectors in backgroundScope; every ViewModel has at least one "sequence of states" test. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not banning Unconfined entirely (it's still useful for collectors). Not adding a UI debounce to hide a modeling bug. Not adding real delays to tests.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would Standard alone have caught it? → Only with fakes that emit at different virtual times; synchronous fakes still collapse. Both matter.
  • What if product wants the partial state? → Then the test asserts it as the contract.
  • Could distinctUntilChanged in combine help? → No; the two states differ.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After a "UI flicker" postmortem the team added time-shaped fakes with configurable latencies. The first run found four more screens with partial-state flashes that no test had ever been able to express.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: delays in fakes only, no dispatcher analysis.
  • Hire: recognizes Unconfined plus synchronous fakes hides sequences; uses Turbine and Standard.
  • Strong hire: also fixes the modeling (Loadable), defines a dispatcher policy, and verifies timing with currentTime.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test logic that depends on time: withTimeout, exponential backoff retries, periodic polling, cache expiry (TTL), and Clock reads? What do you inject and what do you assert on?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Time is the hardest dependency in async code. Seniors design for testability and assert on virtual timestamps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Anything driven by delay, withTimeout, debounce, sample, or timeout runs on the test scheduler and I assert on currentTime. Anything reading wall-clock time (System.currentTimeMillis, Instant.now(), TTL checks) is a hidden dependency, so I inject a Clock or TimeSource, backed in tests by testScheduler.timeSource or a controllable fake. Then I assert exact timestamps: backoff sums, call times, expiry boundaries at TTL-1 and TTL."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Virtual vs wall clock are two worlds. currentTime advances only when the scheduler advances; System.currentTimeMillis() doesn't. Mixing them gives tests where a TTL never expires.
  • Options for wall-clock: (1) kotlin.time.TimeSource injected; in tests use testScheduler.timeSource (comparable marks since 1.7.0). (2) java.time.Clock with a fake that reads currentTime. (3) A fun interface Clock { fun now(): Long } with a lambda { currentTime }.
  • withTimeout(t): virtual, fires when the scheduler reaches t. Test by making the fake suspend longer than t and asserting TimeoutCancellationException and currentTime == t.
  • Retry/backoff: record call timestamps in the fake; assert [0, 500, 1500, 3500] rather than only counts.
  • Polling: use backgroundScope and advanceTimeBy(n * interval), then runCurrent() for the boundary (Q637).
  • Test the boundaries: TTL-1 ms is fresh, TTL ms is expired; both sides of the boundary have off-by-one bugs.
  • Jitter: inject Random with a fixed seed or a function; otherwise assert ranges.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Cache(private val clock: TimeSource.WithComparableMarks, private val ttl: Duration) {
    private var mark: ComparableTimeMark? = null
    fun isFresh() = mark?.let { it.elapsedNow() < ttl } == true
    fun touch() { mark = clock.markNow() }
}

@Test
fun ttl_boundary() = runTest {
    val cache = Cache(testScheduler.timeSource, 10.seconds)
    cache.touch()
    advanceTimeBy(9_999); assertTrue(cache.isFresh())
    advanceTimeBy(1);     assertFalse(cache.isFresh())   // elapsed == ttl
}

@Test
fun backoffTimestamps() = runTest {
    val times = mutableListOf<Long>()
    val api = FakeApi { times += currentTime; throw IOException() }
    launch { runCatching { retryWithBackoff(api) } }
    advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals(listOf(0L, 500L, 1500L, 3500L), times)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• System.currentTimeMillis() in production and delay skipping in tests: expiry logic never triggers.
  • Asserting elapsed in 0..5000 (always true) instead of exact virtual values.
  • Using Instant.now() in the code under test and advanceTimeBy in tests.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is timeSource available on all versions? → Comparable marks via testScheduler.timeSource came with 1.7.0; check the version when targeting older libs.
  2. How do you test sample/debounce? → Same virtual time; mind the boundary.
  3. How do you simulate device clock changes (user changes system time)? → Inject a mutable fake clock; use a monotonic source for durations and a wall-clock source for calendar logic, and test them separately.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "advanceTimeBy." The senior inserts a clock seam, asserts exact timestamps and boundaries, handles jitter, and separates monotonic from wall-clock time.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A token cache used System.currentTimeMillis() with a test that "passed" because expiry never occurred; in production, tokens were reused 30 s past expiry causing 401 spikes at 02:00 every night after the app was backgrounded.

questions.contextHtml:
Incident review. A release shipped with a race in a favorites-sync feature: tapping the heart quickly twice left the server in the wrong state for about 1.8% of toggles (12k affected users in 3 days). Unit coverage of the ViewModel and repository was 91%, all green. The repository:

class FavRepo(private val api: Api, private val scope: CoroutineScope) {
    private var inFlight: Job? = null
    fun toggle(id: String, on: Boolean) {
        inFlight?.cancel()
        inFlight = scope.launch { api.setFavorite(id, on) }
    }
}

Tests used UnconfinedTestDispatcher, a fake API that returns immediately, and one test toggle(id, true); toggle(id, false); assertEquals(false, fakeApi.server[id]). The server state there is correct. In production, api.setFavorite is a Retrofit suspend call: cancelling the first request after it was already sent does not undo it, and the second request can reach the server before the first because of connection pooling and retries.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review for the testing side: why did tests miss it, what do you change in the test strategy, and what is the code fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more tests" or "increase coverage," without addressing that the fake and dispatcher removed the very ordering that mattered.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the API support idempotency keys or version/ETag conditions? What are the acceptable semantics (last tap wins)? Is the order guaranteed server-side? What does the offline mode do?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side fix or client hotfix: send the desired final state with a monotonically increasing client sequence number; add a reconciling refresh after sync completes; support a feature flag to disable the optimistic path if needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Cancel of an in-flight HTTP request is cooperative and non-transactional: the request may already be applied. (b) Out-of-order arrival of two requests. (c) Tests could not represent either: Unconfined plus an immediate fake. (d) Red herring: coroutine cancellation "being broken."
  4. How I'd verify: Write a test with a fake API that has gates per call, and a scheduler-controlled completion order including "request 1 applied but its response cancelled" and "request 2 overtakes request 1"; replay production logs with request ids.
  5. Root cause: Design relied on cancel as a rollback, and the test model was too kind: synchronous completions and eager execution. Coverage measured lines, not interleavings.
  6. Fix: Serialize writes per id, collapse to the latest desired state, and send a sequence/version:
class FavRepo(private val api: Api, scope: CoroutineScope) {
    private val desired = MutableStateFlow<Map<String, Boolean>>(emptyMap())
    init {
        scope.launch {
            desired.collect { map ->          // collect (not collectLatest): never cancel a sent request
                for ((id, on) in map) api.setFavorite(id, on)
            }
        }
    }
    fun toggle(id: String, on: Boolean) = desired.update { it + (id to on) }
}

(Real code would track sent state to avoid resending and handle failures.) Tests with a controllable fake:

@Test fun rapidToggles_endWithLastState() = runTest {
    val api = GatedApi()                        // each call suspends on its own gate
    val repo = FavRepo(api, backgroundScope + StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))
    repo.toggle("1", true); repo.toggle("1", false)
    runCurrent()
    api.completeAll()                           // release in order, then try reversed in another test
    advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals(false, api.server["1"])
}
  1. Prevention: A concurrency test checklist for stateful sync code (overlapping calls, reversed completion, cancellation mid-flight, retry duplicates); a deterministic "interleaving" fake utility; coverage reviews that ask about interleavings, not lines; dispatch policy: Standard for code under test.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not removing cancellation across the board; cancellation is right for reads, wrong for writes. Not relying on the server order alone without idempotency/versioning. Not adding sleeps to "hope" ordering.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can the fake simulate "applied but response lost"? → Yes: apply to server then throw CancellationException or IOException on the gate.
  • Would a Mutex per id be enough? → It serializes in-process but not retries or multiple devices; add versions.
  • How would you test across process death? → Persist pending intent (WorkManager/DB) and test with a fake store; separate chunk of the test pyramid.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The review's biggest finding was cultural: green dashboards on coverage made the team stop asking what the fake could not do. Adding a "what interleavings can't this fake express?" line to the PR template changed the next three designs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "write more tests"; blames cancellation.
  • Hire: identifies non-transactional cancel and the missing interleaving in tests; fix with serialization.
  • Strong hire: gated fakes to control completion order, version/idempotency, distinguishes reads vs writes for cancellation, and proposes process changes (checklist, PR template, dispatcher policy).
